topic: Stomach growling: migrating motor complex cleaning wave, borborygmi, food switches it off
hook: Your gut growls to clean itself

slides.title: Your gut growls to clean itself
slides.body: Between meals, waves of muscle sweep leftover food and bacteria out of your stomach and gut.
slides.image_prompt: Glowing pink tunnel of smooth muscle with a gentle wave rippling through it, tiny crumbs swept along, soft warm light, macro style

slides.title: It runs on a timer
slides.body: Called the migrating motor complex, it repeats roughly every 90 to 120 minutes while you haven't eaten.
slides.image_prompt: Vintage alarm clock beside an empty white plate on a kitchen table, soft morning light, minimal composition

slides.title: The noise is gas
slides.body: The rumble is gas and fluid being squeezed through your intestines. Doctors call it borborygmi.
slides.image_prompt: Air bubbles squeezing through a curved transparent tube filled with liquid, dramatic side lighting, dark background

slides.title: Eating switches it off
slides.body: Food stops the cleaning wave almost at once. A growl means your gut is empty, not that you're starving.
slides.image_prompt: Steaming bowl of soup on a wooden table next to a light switch turned off, cozy warm light

cta: Follow for a new body fact daily
caption:
That rumble in a quiet meeting isn't your stomach begging for food. It's a cleaning cycle called the migrating motor complex: every 90 to 120 minutes on an empty stomach, muscle waves sweep leftovers and bacteria down your gut.

The sound itself comes from gas and fluid being pushed along, and the first bite of food switches the whole cycle off. Follow @you.didnot.know for a new body fact every day.
